core_summary: This chapter builds the foundation of plane geometry from primitive geometric concepts (points, line segments, rays, lines) to the quantitative measurement of rotation in degrees. It covers rotation turns (full, half, quarter), classification of angles (acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex), protractor usage, paper-folding constructions for perpendiculars and angle bisectors, and angular properties of clock hands and circular central divisions.
key_concepts: Geometric Primitives: A point has zero dimensions; a line segment has definite length and two endpoints; a ray extends endlessly in one direction from an initial point; a line extends endlessly in two directions.
Uniqueness of Straight Lines: Exactly one unique straight line passes through any two distinct points, whereas infinitely many lines pass through a single point.
Angle as Rotation Measure: An angle quantifies the amount of turn between two rays sharing a vertex, independent of the drawn length of the rays.
Full Rotation & Fractional Degree Conversion: One full rotation equals 360°. A fraction 'f' of a full turn equals f x 360°.
Classification of Angles: Acute (0° < theta < 90°), Right (theta = 90°), Obtuse (90° < theta < 180°), Straight (theta = 180°), Reflex (180° < theta < 360°).
Paper Folding Symmetry: Folding a straight line crease onto itself forms perpendicular lines meeting at 4 right angles (90°). Folding an angle so its arms overlap creates an angle bisector.

key_terms.definition: A precise location in space represented by a dot, possessing zero length, width, or depth.
The shortest straight path connecting two distinct endpoints, having a measurable length.
A straight path starting at a fixed initial endpoint and extending endlessly in one direction.
A continuous one-dimensional straight path extending infinitely in both opposite directions.
A ray that divides an angle into two equal adjacent angles of identical degree measure.
Two lines that intersect at a right angle (90°).

key_takeaways: Angle magnitude depends exclusively on rotation divergence, not on arm length.
Clock hour marks divide 360° into 12 equal 30° divisions.
Paper folding provides an empirical geometric method to construct perpendiculars and angle bisectors.
